prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which established the incretin principle underlying treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange did not change my view that B025 is the right single achievement, and the chair's summary confirms that the shared ground is substantive: Drucker and Holst are in all six trios, and the evidence arc from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect to large independent outcome trials leaves no maturity question. My remaining task is the third seat. I keep Mojsov because the identification of GLP-1(7-36) as the biologically active, insulinotropic form is the step that turned a gene-encoded sequence into a defined hormone, and that is a discovery-stage contribution on which both the later physiology and the later pharmacology depended. A citation worded around physiology and the active form is coherent and defensible, and it asks the committee to reward what was found rather than who built the product.
statement.case_against: The case against my own trio is real. Mojsov's priority is disputed, Habener is not among the credited names, and I cannot verify the priority evidence from the supplied credit alone. Leaving out Knudsen means the citation honours the biology but not the molecule that reached patients, and three colleagues argue that this omission misreads why the field matters. I also accept Svenningsson's point that half-life extension through acylation and albumin binding was a mechanistic insight and not only industrial optimisation, so the line I draw between discovery and development is a judgment, not a fact. If the committee reads the prize as physiology plus therapy, my trio is the wrong one.

responses.point: The chair argues that Knudsen's fatty-acid-acylated, albumin-binding analogues solved the specific biological problem of DPP-4 degradation and short half-life, so they are a discovery in their own right, and that the citation should name both physiology and development.
responses.response: This moved me on the description of Knudsen's work, which I had called translational and which is better described as applied mechanism. It did not move me on the seat. The half-life problem was defined by Drucker's and Holst's own work on DPP-4 degradation and GLP-1 action, so the analogue work builds on the physiology that two of the three laureates already represent. A citation naming both parts would, at three seats, have to omit either the active-peptide identification or the drug design, and I find the first omission harder to explain because it concerns the identity of the hormone itself. I would accept your trio if the committee settles the Mojsov priority question against her.

responses.point: Perlmann prefers Knudsen because Mojsov's priority is disputed in a way he cannot resolve from the record, and he does not want a prize to rest on a contested claim when a documented contribution is available.
responses.response: That is the strongest argument for his trio and I take it seriously. A contested priority is a risk, but the dispute concerns who was first and how much credit each group deserves, not whether the active-form identification happened or mattered. The same dispute also touches Habener, who we cannot name, so replacing Mojsov with Knudsen avoids the argument without repairing the gap it leaves in the record. I would change my vote if the committee concludes that the evidence supports no credited role for Mojsov in establishing GLP-1(7-36) as the active form, but contested is not the same as unsupported.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps Knudsen because the Nobel tradition in this category has honoured the step that turns a mechanism into a medicine, and she would accept the Mojsov variant only if the priority question is settled with Habener.
responses.response: The tradition argument is fair, but the prizes that rewarded a therapeutic step usually did so for the discovery of a principle that the therapy then embodied. Here the principle is incretin biology and the active peptide, and semaglutide and liraglutide are applications of it. I agree that the priority question cannot be settled by this committee from the supplied material, and I do not think we should pretend otherwise in the citation, which is why I would word it around the physiology and the active form and not around who was first. I also note your broader point that the drug design is what made the field matter, and I do not minimise it.

responses.point: Linnarsson shares the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio but concedes the Knudsen case is closer than he first allowed, and still ranks cGAS-STING above CAR-T on conceptual grounds.
responses.response: On GLP-1 I now hold the position with less confidence than I did in round 1, and I agree that the choice between our trio and the chair's is a judgment about framing, not a scientific error on either side. On cGAS-STING I still differ. A clean mechanism is real, but after more than a decade without an approved STING-directed drug, and with five credited names that cannot be cut to Chen and Barber without losing Ishikawa, Sun or Wu, I do not think it is ready to share a prize. CAR-T has the direct clinical consequence that cGAS-STING does not yet have, so I keep B047 ahead of it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen takes the third seat; I hold Mojsov with moderate confidence and cannot verify the priority evidence, including Habener's role, from the supplied credit.
Whether the committee frames B025 as physiology and the active peptide or as physiology plus therapy; the citation wording decides which trio is defensible.
Whether a second part is worth adding at all, since under the three-person cap any second achievement would shrink the GLP-1 trio below the people the committee most wants to credit.
If a second achievement were pursued, whether CAR-T is defensible without Eshhar and with or without Rosenberg, and how three of six optogenetics names could be chosen.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have documented co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen, neither of whom is credited on a shortlisted ballot. My RNA-processing work is thematically near B020 (antisense splicing), but I have no documented collaboration with its credited names and it is not in my configuration, so I see no ground for recusal.
